newsitem.title: USA: GM realigns car management, names training chief.
newsitem.headline: GM realigns car management, names training chief.

text.p: General Motors Corp. realigned the top management of its North American passenger car operations Monday, shifting small car development chief Richard "Skip" LeFauve to lead the company's new "General Motors University."

Donald Hackworth, currently vice president and group executive in charge of mid-size and luxury cars, will assume responsibility for small cars in GM's North American Operations, including GM's Saturn unit.
Hackworth will get a new title -- vice president and group executive, NAO Car Group -- but GM does not plan a broad consolidation of the small and mid-size/luxury car units.

LeFauve told reporters Monday that the two groups will continue to maintain separate engineering and administrative staffs, but will continue to increase their cooperation with GM's other global product groups.
"I wouldn't anticipate a lot of changes in small car for some time," LeFauve said.
Executives previously reporting to LeFauve will now report to Hackworth, including Saturn President Donald Hudler, who assumes LeFauve's title as Saturn chairman.

As head of the GM University, LeFauve will be responsible for creating an institution that will train the auto giant's future leaders and foster more cooperation among its far-flung global operations.

LeFauve was named senior vice president for global leadership development and global human resources processes. He remains on GM's influential Global Strategy Board and reports to GM Vice Chairman Harry Pearce.

The university will be based at GM's new headquarters in Detroit's riverfront Renaissance Center complex, but will offer classes for executives, engineers and other salaried staff at GM locations throughout the world and via videoconferencing and Internet technologies.

The university, began offering classes in April 1996 and about 400 GM executives have attended classes so far. GM has identified more than 3,800 executives and 1,000 "high potential" young employees for training.
Classes will be taught by other GM executives, professors from top business schools and by contract training providers and think-tanks.
LeFauve said one of his main goals is to help GM develop common systems and practices for engineering and other business activities throughout the world.

One recent effort has been to put GM's North American and European engineers on common design systems and tools. Previously, critical data such as key vehicle dimensions were measured differently and would not translate between German and American engineers, making joint car programs difficult.

LeFauve said the new training initiative also is aimed at transforming GM from a "knowing organization" to a "learning organization," erasing some of the company's hide-bound, sometimes arrogant corporate culture, which nearly smothered the automaker in the early 1990s.
The university is separate from the now-independent GMI Institute, a fully accredited four-year engineering college in Flint, Mich., which GM founded as the General Motors Institute.
